utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: This hearing is taking place in the absence of the accused. It has become unavoidable that we have a hearing in his absence because there are administrative matters of such a nature that they must be dealt with in order that witnesses can be informed and the like and the timetable arranged. We're grateful that Mr. Tapuskovic has been able to be with us, representing the amici in this matter. I will see that a copy of the transcript of this hearing is served on the accused in the Detention Unit so that he knows what's gone on in his absence. Mr. Nice, there are matters, I understand, you wish to raise about the -- about witnesses in particular.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes. First of all, in order that the record can inform the accused and simply so that all aspects of the case are covered, I appear today assisted by my learned friends Mr. Ryneveld, Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff, and also Ms. Harris in respect of the Bosnia component of the case, as Mr. Groome is absent; and of course I'm assisted as ever by Ms. Graham, the case manager, but that's the total representation here. Your Honour, I hope that the Court has now received a witness list dated the 25th of June.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We've just received that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'll perhaps take you through it because it's designed to be helpful and I hope it is.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters don't have the list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The interpreters don't have the list. It may be helpful if they had it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It's coming their way. And the Court should also have had an earlier document in landscape format with some comments on the front of it which really stand as a form of skeleton argument, I suppose.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: In relation to the 11 witnesses --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, we have had that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And obviously that can't be discussed further in the absence of the accused.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: But we've set out our position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That's in relation to -- so it's clear for the record, that's in relation to the 11 witnesses who you apply -- who you have applied for to be heard without cross-examination, I shouldn't say to be heard, to be introduced without cross-examination under Rule 92 bis. You should, while we're dealing with that, have received an order in relation to two of those.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, we have. The order and our document crossed in the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: -- in the filing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That was, if I recollect, K24 and K31. They, we have said, should be present.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, indeed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: For cross-examination. But the others, we have to rule on. It's one of the matters we need to timetable.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, before we come to these lists and other matters of detail, can I, for personal reasons, ask for not indulgence but some assistance? If we do sit tomorrow because the accused is fit to sit, I would ask that we deal with matters of evidence and not procedure because I'm not intending to be here. Likewise next week, if the accused is fit to sit, we have evidence to fill the entire week, but I'm intending to be away on something that will be difficult to cancel for the Tuesday and Wednesday, and I'd ask, therefore, that procedural matters not be taken before the Thursday. The second point I would make in general is this: Following the first week of absence of the accused - that's last week, or indeed in the middle of it - we inquired or had inquired as to whether the week of July ending on the 2nd of August might be available. We had originally understood that it might be available and people have made appropriate arrangements to hold themselves in readiness, not to be taking holidays on that week and so on. And up and until the end of last week's absence by the accused through ill health, it was at least possible that we could have got all or very nearly all of the Kosovo-only related evidence in by the 2nd of August without having to apply for any further time. His continuing ill health and the loss of two further days, I'm afraid, makes that, difficult though it would have been, now impossible, and we will inevitably be asking for some time, a rather limited amount of time, in September. We would also be assisted to know if that last week is going to be available because people do have plans that they've made and to some degree unmade, and it will obviously assist us to know where we stand in relation to that week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, let us consider all that together while we can. Is there anything else relevant to those decisions you want to raise with us?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Sorry, decisions about timing?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: No. I think that's it. I mean, I'm not making the application for extension yet because I will come to that when we look at the amount of evidence there is outstanding.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It may be convenient if you make the application for extension now. The point is this: That what we need to do as soon as possible is to timetable the matter through to the autumn.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Certainly, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: And it would be convenient to deal with it together.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Let me then deal with it in general terms and then we'll look at the list in particular. When we've been optimistic about the possibility of finishing all the Kosovo -- exclusively Kosovo-related evidence by the 26th of July or, as we later thought, the 2nd of August, we had in mind first of all the clear indications from the Chamber that it would prefer evidence that dealt with more than one of the three indictments to be heard after August, and we'd factored that in in respect of most but not all of our insider witnesses, and we had planned to incorporate before the August break three insider witnesses, one of whom undoubtedly covers events on all three indictments and two of whom do to a degree but who are much more specific to Kosovo. But we had decided to seek to call those three ahead of August for several reasons, and in large part those reasons still hold good. They include that very considerable arrangements have already been made, difficult arrangements, to get those witnesses to be in a position to give evidence before August at inconvenience and it may be risk to themselves, so that for human reasons it's a good idea to have them heard when they are originally expecting to be heard. Second, and perhaps almost most importantly, their giving evidence is likely to be very significant or certainly significant for other potential insider witnesses for there is no doubt but that the giving of evidence by insiders in this case, as they are called, will free up other similarly placed potential witnesses to give evidence, and evidence from such witnesses should not only improve significantly and rapidly the quality of evidence before the Chamber but should ultimately bring dividends in terms of time, or could ultimately bring dividends in terms of the time the case will take because obviously the more access one has to close insider witnesses, the less is there the need to rely on other categories of evidence. So we very much wanted to call these three witnesses for that particular reason, and that remains our view. Knowing that we must make an application for evidence now to be heard in September in relation to Kosovo generally simply because we've lost so much time through ill health that, in our respectful submission, it simply couldn't conceivably be right to try to hold us to either the 26th or the 2nd of August, we've given thought to whether we should change our view in relation to these three witnesses and put them back to September, October, or something like that, and we would very much prefer not to, for the reasons I've given, and would suggest that this will in no way prejudice the accused and indeed will probably serve to assist him, given that the summer break is intended, in large part, to be the period of time when he prepares for the next part of the trial. If we -- first of all, let's assume that the accused is fit enough to be in court for the remaining days, which is by no means certain, I suppose. But if he is and if we're able to get those three witnesses here - and there's many a slip for this type of witness between intention and reality, but if we are able to get them here - then three significant witnesses will have been dealt with by the accused and the residue in respect of which we will be making an application for Kosovo will be crime-base witnesses almost exclusively, a category of witness which it must be easier for him to prepare, as he's shown us by his ability to prepare for these witnesses sometimes, as he himself has announced, overnight. It would be much easier for him to prepare and thus less demanding on him. So that to take these, or to plan to take these insider witnesses ahead of the summer break will distribute the difficult work for him and enable him perhaps to make a more even and better use of his time and should not inconvenience him at all. So that our intention remains to call those three witnesses, although, when we look at the timetable, we'll have to be ready to allow for the possibility that for different reasons, one or other of them may not attend. The next matter that may affect the timetable is Rule 70 witnesses. The Chamber has outstanding the issue of the one particular Rule 70 witness for whom certain conditions were sought by the providing government and in respect of whom -- I hope you've now been provided with the text provided by that government.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, we have.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It was late. It was my fault that it was late. I didn't get permission and overlooked it. That's obviously got to be discussed and decided about, and we've built him in, but as I've been explaining throughout the last six months or something, there are other Rule 70 witnesses in respect of whom we have no agreement with the providing government, at least no agreement -- no, we have no agreement. Things may be changing. They may change independently of the decision about the particular witness that the Chamber has to make, a decision in the course of which no doubt Rule 70 will be given a somewhat detailed examination. They may change independently. They may change as a result of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let us pause there. I think we have not made our Scheduling Order sufficiently clear on Rule 70. We will need to timetable a discussion on Rule 70, probably sooner rather than later. The issue is one which we must deal with. But so that you know what we are concerned about, the issue which we wish you to address - it would be helpful if you did it in writing - is whether Rule 70 applies at all. The issue is: Is this a Rule 70 matter at all? And if so, it's for you to establish why. And I don't think we made that sufficiently clear in our Scheduling Order, and it's that to which we'd be grateful to have your submissions.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I was first alerted the day before yesterday and yesterday to the expectation of written submissions and we will attend to that as soon as we can. And I'm certainly assisted by having confirmation of that which I expected, namely, that the Chamber's looking at the issue rather in a root and branch -- on a root and branch basis, and that may indeed, if not assist resolution of the other witnesses as well as the instant witness, certainly sharpen the debate that is going on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I think one could take it a bit further and say this: Is this not really an issue of confidence, confidential matter which the government does not wish to have disclosed? Which is a slightly different point to Rule 70 which deals specifically with information. What it seems that the government are concerned about is that other information, or information outside what's given in the statement and in the original information, shouldn't be disclosed. That seems to be a different point to Rule 70.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Those observations are extremely helpful and they will find themselves winging their way on a transcript, in due course today, to the government concerned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That is the issue which we have to address, the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: To take the matter further, to try and assist, the other Rule which has to be considered is 54 bis, if I recollect, if I've got the number rightly.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. I think it only concerns documents, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Not just documents. It also deals with information.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. It's orders directly to states for the production of documents. But indeed we have got that in mind and we will review the position. Of course, with Rule 70, there's been a history of dealings between the Tribunal and one or more governments, and that has given rise to expectations perhaps on both sides, and I'm not at all disheartened to hear that the matter may now be under review. But the Chamber's observations are helpful and confirm my -- not my optimism but confirm my expectation that the debate about Rule 70 may have an effect on whether I am able to call one or other of the other so-called Rule 70 witnesses. But as I've said, there may also be other independent events that will lead to one or more of those witnesses becoming available. Now, of those witnesses, one at least is exclusively Kosovo connected and would take a significant amount of time to deal with - not an extended amount but a significant amount of time - and is likely to be a witness, I would forecast, from whom the Chamber might want to hear. So that a couple of days, it might be thought, should be borne in mind as days possibly to be allocated to one of those witnesses. Now, with that in mind, can I invite the Chamber to look at the latest list, prepared yesterday in light of what we knew yesterday about the accused's state of health. We had to send back nearly all the witnesses who have been waiting here for a fortnight and more. And before I pass from that, the Chamber may know from other sources and will, I hope, accept from me that the business of waiting for the opportunity to give evidence for these witnesses is a pretty difficult experience. They are kept in a hotel that in many ways might as well be in the middle of nowhere because they don't, by and large, speak English; and the Victims and Witnesses Unit is terrific in what it does for them but the process is an isolated and difficult one where they have nothing to do except revisit their memories. And I mention that because if you'd be good enough to look at the list numbers 1 to 4, numbers 1, 3, and 4 are three listed witnesses who have been here a fortnight and who we have been able to retain, they having come a very long distance to be here, and we hope that if the Court reconvenes tomorrow with the accused present, their evidence may be given. You'll also notice number 2, the same name as number 1. Number 2 was, until comparatively recently, a listed witness, but in one of the processes of reducing witnesses in order to try and reduce the time the case would take, his name was deleted. He is indeed the son of number 1, and he's been here all these weeks as the person looking after number 1, his father, who is in different or rather poor health. Number 2, whose material has been served on the accused, is like many of the people who come here, of course, anxious to give evidence. His personal tragedy was to have his wife and all three of his children killed in the course of the events that both he and his father can speak of. Now, we've seen that these witnesses are cross-examined by the accused, typically, and therefore, if time allows tomorrow, given that his material has been served and given that he is here and assuming that issues will be raised in relation to this the Prosecution would say appalling event at Milos Gilic Street, we would ask tomorrow -- it can't be done today because the accused isn't here to respond, but I forecast the application -- we would ask for him to be taken as well if that could be accommodated within the day. But otherwise, it will be 1, 3, and 4 tomorrow which we hope will consume the day, with or without the addition of number 2.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The information we have is that a hearing tomorrow is unlikely, although we'll, of course, make further inquiries. Pausing there and in case I forget, we have not yet had a medical report for this week. We had one for the week before. We have not had one for this week. We order that one be provided.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. We are concerned, if we may say so, about the specificity already provided in the report. Of course it's a matter for the Chamber, but ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The first one was in a fairly scrappy form but it did indicate there was an illness and what it was and how long he would be off. Since then, we've had nothing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I'm told there was a perfunctory report filed yesterday which we will have in front of us.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The Chamber won't be surprised to know that the Prosecution is not only concerned that there should be specificity given to these medical reports but is prepared to be cautious if not skeptical in due course if these things go on too regularly. Perhaps if I say no more about it --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That is matter for the Trial Chamber. We will get a report. We have, of course, to rely upon the doctor and his decisions of diagnosis about the accused.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, 1 to 4 or 1, 3, and 4, if they can't be taken tomorrow, create a difficult logistical problem, the resolution to which is probably to send them somewhere between now and next week and to seek to take them next Thursday, removing from the list whoever is presently on next Thursday's list. Then if we go down the list, we come at number 5 and 6 to Tuesday, and these are fixed-date witnesses, 2nd and 3rd of July. And then we go through some more witnesses from Djakovica, 7, 8, 9. 10 Suva Reka, and then 11 Sandra Mitchell, who, I think, has timetable problems that mean she must really be available on the 4th of July. Obviously, if the accused is not going to be available tomorrow, all of this part of the list may have to be somewhat amended. 13, Mr. Vollebaek, comes for the 8th and 9th of July; and then K25 follows on with another name, number 15, on the 10th of July. I don't think there's any remaining difficulty about naming him but there have been some Rule 70 or similar difficulties there so I won't, for the time being, name him publicly. Dr. Baccard returns briefly, we would forecast, on the 15th of July with more witnesses named there, insiders of a lower category, and then Djakovica witnesses to follow. That brings us, in our calculations, over the page at 21, to the middle of July roughly. It's probably not realistic to put it much more precisely than that. There's then the report of Philip Coo and the military expert General Sir Peter de la Billiere, who of course relate only to Kosovo and in respect of one of whom there is challenges to part of his conclusions which will have to be dealt with.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. That is in relation to Mr. Coo. Pausing there, we will need to timetable that fairly soon for discussion. As part of his report, there's reference to the OSCE Blue Book, and we've recently been provided with copies of it. That would seem to be a helpful document which could be exhibited.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Perhaps you can make arrangements to secure that when we're back in open session, as it were. The military expert I see, the second military expert for the moment I will refer to him, I see a draft report will be available today.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: He deals with different issues to Mr. Coo.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: He does indeed, yes, and it's explained why. One at the high level, experience of command and so on, and observations about the inevitable interrelation of different armed forces, different entirely from Mr. Coo's. And this combination of experts is not without precedent, I think, in this Tribunal. One could not in any way expect the military expert, the general, to be dealing with the mass of material, the mass of military material that is dealt with by Mr. Coo. It would be asking the impossible and quite unreasonable. But in any event, they bring different skills to bear on the same material, and we would invite the Chamber to say in due course, obviously when the matter is ventilated, that they are properly complementary and in no sense duplicative. And it's very important in a case like this to have a high level military expert to deal with the issues that inevitably arise when one's dealing with a defendant of the former position of this accused. But in dealing with those issues, you can't overlook the functional issues lower down that Mr. Coo deals with and deals with in great detail. But perhaps we can return to that topic sufficiently ahead of any travel arrangements that Sir Peter de la Billiere will be making to make sure that we satisfy you that that is an appropriate course to take. That's not unprecedented at all and I think it's, in some ways, a standard procedure in some other trials. Your Honour, we then come to 24, 25, and 26, the three insiders to whom I have referred, each allocated several days. And assuming that all arrangements are in place, and the Chamber may know from some of the ex parte filings what some of those intended arrangements are, assuming those arrangements are in place, we will probably nevertheless have to at least give some thought to having reserves of crime-base witnesses at whatever inconvenience to those witnesses to allow for the possibility of the evidence going short and time becoming available. But one way or another, those witnesses will take us to the 26th of July. Now, obviously, if there's another week between the 26th of July and the 2nd of August, then some of what follows can be -- might be accommodated within August, but please remember what I've already said about one of the Rule 70 witnesses: We are anticipating the possibility of a change whereby he will become available and have already made a request, if so, that he be available within this period of time. Obviously, other witnesses would have to be put back if the Chamber were minded to take his evidence and assuming that he's free, which I don't know, and all assuming that it's possible to call him. So those uncertainties, I'm afraid, are bound to continue and we can only do our best to tell you what they are. So subject to all of those, we then come to K31 and 24 in respect of whom the Chamber's already made its ruling. Then number 29. And if you go straight over to the next page but one, page 8, and starting at 43, you've then got 27, 28, 29, and then starting at 43 and going on through to page 10, number 50, that's the collection of witnesses dealt with in the other document in respect of whom we say cross-examination may not be necessary and they could be fully bis'd. And the Chamber may remember from the document that we provided, our calculation is that those witnesses - so that would be 27, 28, 29, and then 43, 44, 45, 46, 47, 48, 49 and 50 - would take some three days if they were to be cross-examined. So that's our calculation. So that would leave the intervening page, page 7, as witnesses who simply have had to be put back by reason of the accused's ill health. We've put them back in that position. They are crime-base witnesses and so one can give a rough calculation of two or three per day to see that three or so days will be required for them, would be required for them. And if we then go over to page 8, starting with number 37, there's a witness subject to argument who would probably take the best part of a day, and then one of numbers R3 to 7, as I've already explained, will probably take a couple of days. So -- and then just moving on to page 10, everything that follows from 51 and onwards is reference to a witness who covers not just Kosovo --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I thought we indicated a view about 51.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You indicated a view, and if the court remembers, it was a provisional view and I said that what we would like to do, please, is to put him back because he can cover more than Kosovo, take a fuller statement, detailing other matters, reconsider our position and apply or complete the application in respect of him at a later stage of the trial. So we had sought to leave that unresolved and I understood that that approach had been acceptable to the Chamber. So everything else that follows, if it's available, will fall to be dealt with, in line with the Court's indication, after the summer break. But there's one matter of detail I should deal with and that's at page 13, number 60, and K38 in respect of whom the court has indicated provisionally - K38 at page 11 - indicated not yet satisfied that he's a witness whose evidence should be admitted. K38's evidence could be rather more wide than just financial matters but is closely integrated with financial matters, indeed central to financial matters in some way. Where is he? At the moment, he's -- I'm sure I've got the right number. 53 on page 11. But the Chamber indicated that we weren't allowed to call him at the moment, subject to further argument. Now, it could be that we could put back all of the argument about financial evidence, for there seems to be some challenge to that, and about K38, until the autumn or later because that evidence will inevitably be heard, if at all, in the later parts of this trial. We would prefer, if time allowed, to have the argument about the financial evidence before the summer break and to further address you about K38. We prefer to do that for two reasons --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just one moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We prefer to deal with the matter, if time were available, before the summer break for two reasons: One, because there's further work to be done in respect of financial evidence, which is, of course, extremely complex and difficult to deal with; and secondly, quite frankly, because if for any reason Mr. Torkildsen was going to be excluded, which we would argue would be quite wrong if he were to be excluded from giving evidence, the sooner he knows, the better because he can return to get on with his job as a financial investigator in Norway. He's here for this case. So in an ideal world, if time is available, we would rather argue certainly the financial report and any questions as to its admissibility before the summer break, and we would then probably seek to bring in further argument about K38 responsive to your latest ruling. But there is only so much one can fit into any container, and I suspect that if the options are between procedural matters that may be adjourned if only to the end of August or beginning of September and taking evidence, the Chamber's choice may be to take evidence wherever possible because of its understandable desire to get as much evidence done as early as possible, a desire which we entirely share and always have done. So there, in a rather extended way, is the range of problems that we are facing. As I hope the Chamber will have seen from looking at this list, the amount of evidence outstanding on our plan, subject to resolution of the witnesses who might not be cross-examined and subject to the one Rule 70 so-called witness, is actually quite limited. It's a week or so as at present appears.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: A week or so beyond the 26th of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Taking that as the date so we can consider the matter, you reckon that by the 26th of July there should be something like a week or perhaps two, a week or two outstanding.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. It will get longer if any of the procedural discussions take a lot of time or if witnesses take longer than expected. It will be less if one of the K witnesses that we intend to call, one of the three insider witnesses we intend to call before the summer recess can't be called then, because once they can't be called before the summer recess then there may be no particular reason to call them as part of the discrete Kosovo evidence. It may simply be sensible to put them back to a generally later date. But for the reasons I've given earlier, we would very much prefer to try and stick with our plan of calling them before the summer recess and believe that will bring dividends to the trial generally if we are able to do so. But each of them -- and I should say this, incidentally, that one of the particular reasons for asking the Court to deal with these matters in so far as it can in the absence of the accused today is that, for each of them, I think there's now a 20-day disclosure order. We'd sought an extended order in respect of the accused, from 10 to 20 days for one of them, because we could see that it was a difficult witness that might have required longer than the ten days he typically was allowed. I think, actually, 20 days has been allowed for all three and perhaps quite understandably, but that means we will have to serve their material, thus revealing all the details about them, pretty well this weekend at the latest if we are to call them at the times planned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Before we consider the timetable, we ought also to consider what procedural matters are outstanding.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Under two headings: One, outstanding for Kosovo; two, outstanding for Bosnia and Croatia because we have to begin the consideration of those parts --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: -- fairly soon. And therefore, we should set aside time in the timetable for those matters. Okay. It may be of assistance if I have a note, if I read out the note of the matters which I have which need to be resolved. The Rule 70 issue, the exhibit to Dr. Baccard's statement on which I think we now have your final -- your latest submission.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: They were served yesterday. I hope they are sufficient in themselves to deal with the matter. We are obviously available to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It may be that could be dealt with without oral argument.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Maybe. We'll look at that. But certainly the Rule 70 issue has got to be resolved. The issue of Dr. -- Mr. Coo's statement, arguments about admissibility. That will have to be subject of oral argument. The application for the nine 92 bis witnesses. At what stage do you invite us to deal with that? Do we need to deal with that fairly promptly or can we leave that until a later time?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I think providing we keep an eye on travel problems, that can be put back until after the witnesses who give the primary evidence in relation to those particular sites have all been heard.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, clearly it would be convenient and much easier, more practical to deal with that after we've heard the live evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes, certainly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: And the financial evidence which you have raised. I think realistically we are not probably going to have time to deal with that. It's going to be a major issue and going to require thought and consideration with respect to argument.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Certainly, if there's root and branch objection to it coming from any source which can't be immediately set aside, then, yes, I think it will have to be considered in some detail because, of course, the problem about financial evidence is -- financial analysis is that the alternative to dealing with it in the way it's dealt with here would be to call an enormous number of witnesses, or to seek to call an enormous number of witnesses. What is, I think, really a very important component of this case. So perhaps if I might respectfully propose it, if it's not to be heard before the summer, it might prudently be listed for fairly early in the next session, in the early autumn, so that consequential steps can be taken one way or another, depending on the outcome. While I'm speaking --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That would be sensible. Yes. We think it would be sensible. Let us decide now to deal with that in the early autumn. Again, it should be dealt with in September, if possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It seems to me I can save -- we can probably save time by getting in a written submission about Rule 70, especially in light of the helpful observations made this morning. It will take us a few days to do that, but that will cut down the amount of time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Can we say seven days.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Written submissions, seven days.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The other thing that the Chamber might want just to have in the back of its mind is it has indicated a representative of the government concerned might address it. A transcript detailing that has gone to the government concerned. They are willing, but obviously we'll have to fix any hearing with their availability in mind, although I think they will hold themselves out to be available at very short notice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That really means, unless there's something I've overlooked, that the only outstanding matter if we deal with Dr. Baccard's exhibit on the -- on the papers, the outstanding argument really is Mr. Coo and Rule 70 yet to be at some stage, a future time, to be dealt with. So that's something which could be fitted in fairly simply, I would have thought, as convenient, provided we don't overlook it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. And certainly within the next fortnight, assuming that -- assuming that the accused is here for that fortnight. And that fortnight, of course, is a short fortnight because we don't sit next Monday and I think the following week we don't sit on the Thursday and Friday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. And we've lost the Court in afternoon too that week.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can I just mention a couple of tiny but potentially significant other little procedural matters that I want resolved? One -- they both really relate to cooperation by the accused, or require cooperation by the accused and/or by his associates if he is prepared to instruct them to cooperate. First, there's the Rule 68 exercise. The Chamber may know that in the associated case of Sainovic and others, we had a meeting with the lawyers representing those accused, explained the history of Rule 68 disclosure in this case, provided them with the documents showing what we've done, and proposed a way forward. We haven't yet heard back from them, but there was certainly no indication that they aren't prepared to cooperate and make this absolutely critical exercise we have to go through a practical one in this case. At the same time, we raised with them the issue of translations which, of course, we know has arisen in rather stark form in another it may be said associated case of Krajisnik and Plavsic. In that other case, procedures are in place for translations to be acceptable when provided not by CLSS, which is so overburdened, but by other language speakers working for the OTP here and indeed elsewhere. And the procedure with which the Chamber will be familiar is that the translations which might otherwise be thought to be draft translations are sent to Novi Sad university where they are checked on behalf of the defendants concerned, and I gather the strike rate of agreement is something like 94 per cent or thereabouts, 95 per cent. The balance, where there's any doubt about the translation of a particular document or part of a document is then sent to CLSS and the matter is resolved in that way. And this is saving an enormous amount of time and, I suppose, money, but certainly time, and leading to documents being translated for use by the Court much more swiftly. It requires the cooperation of the relevant accused, or at least it may be thought to require. I'm not actually sure that it does because all that's required is that the accused has documents in a language he understands and so on. So I don't believe there's any statutory or other regulatory demand that translations coming from CLSS but it's obviously to be expected those will be the definitive translations were there any issue. And we would be much assisted by the cooperation of the accused, or if he can't cooperate, by his associates insofar as they're able to act on his behalf, in relation to both the translation issue for Bosnia and Croatia, as they are upcoming, and in respect of the Rule 68 exercise generally. We have been able to make telephone contact with them, and they have simply told us that they don't have instructions -- I doubt they used the word "instructions," but that's what it amounts to; they don't have instructions from the accused and therefore they can't attend on meetings with us. We would be grateful if the Court would consider what the position of the associates is, given that they are now recognised by the Tribunal, and consider to what extent the Chamber can perhaps assist in resolving these two issues via the accused and/or the associates.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: See if we follow the problem. It's true that we're familiar with the difficulties which have arisen in Krajisnik about translation. Do I understand it that there are similar problems arising in this case?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, the problems are not similar in the sense that a totally different time period for preparation from that identified by Your Honour in the ruling in relation to Plavsic/Krajisnik as the -- one of the factors that led to the order that was made, but of course similar in that there is an overlap of documents and there are a large number of documents yet to be translated. Of course we're going to be selective and, we hope, very focused in the documents that are to be translated, but there's absolutely no doubt but that CLSS is not capable of delivering all the translations required by all the different parts of this institution. And if there is an acceptable method of getting translations done more swiftly than CLSS could arrange, and less expensive labour in financial terms, then perhaps it ought to be adopted for cases like this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: This is -- is this partly the documents which are part of your case, your documents?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes, they are our documents as well as documents that are common. So that we may find ourselves in the position -- we will find ourselves in the position of having documents that have been dealt with by, if I can use the shorthand, the Novi Sad system and that will be acceptable in that case and there's really no reason --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Why should they not he acceptable in this case?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Precisely. The only reason they might not be is, of course, in that case, the accused have been agreeable to the process.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: As you rightly point out, the point is that it's translated into a language which the accused understands. The method of translation is not prescribed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: As I say, that will be -- that observation on its own is of great assistance to us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I speak for myself, but it would seem to be the important thing is to get it translated.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And then the Rule 68 problem you're familiar with, but we do -- we don't require but the accused's interests will be better served by him, and I'm quite happy to have a meeting with him on the topic -- it's not a problem, he speaks English, or he can have an interpreter. I'm quite happy to have a meeting with him on the topic, along with the amici, to make sure that the parameters we're setting for our Rule 68 searches are the approach ones. I remember at an early stage in this trial Your Honour made the observation that the accused had heard our making the offer to him to contribute to this process, and indeed to make any particular requests for Rule 68 material documents that he might think we had, and I'm concerned that he shouldn't deny himself the opportunity of helping himself in this way. The amici took the view, quite understandably, that there was little point in them having a meeting with us without the accused's representative if there was a prospect of those representatives or the accused himself taking part at some stage. Once it becomes clear that -- if it becomes clear that he's not prepared to cooperate at all, then the second best option is, of course, for us to discuss the matter with the amici alone if they are prepared to do that. I think they probably will be. I've taken some time. I think --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. That was one problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I think that's all I've got to raise. I'll just check with everybody else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The other matter we should deal with is to -- we need to consider, is fixing a Pre-Trial Conference, which I think it will be, for Bosnia and Croatia. I think that rule will apply although technically the trial has started, but we have not yet ruled at all on those components, those indictments.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: No. Your Honour's quite right. Obviously we're somewhat making up procedures as we go along, given the joint trial and the circumstances in which it arose, but Your Honour's quite right. That ought to happen and, I suppose, frankly, it ought to happen before the summer having further inevitable consequences on the available time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. I mean, we ought to fix that. We ought to fix a date and a time for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can I ask that we fix it other than for a date when we've got one of our fixed-date witnesses coming in? At least, as at present advice. It should always be possible to change the date comparatively easily.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It would be sensible to leave at least one hour, and possibly more. I don't know if you have any views about how long it might take. We have started work -- we've been much assisted by the legal officers and we've started work on the preparation. It will obviously take a bit longer before we're ready to contemplate such an exercise.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It's likely to be at least one session. It might go longer, I would have thought. I'm trying to find my list now. I've lost my list for available dates, but if we -- if the Court wanted it in the middle of July, and I hope I won't be -- well, I hope if I get it wrong and that those who deal with the listing of witnesses think I've chosen a wholly incorrect date, I'll be allowed to come back and propose a variation, but it may actually be something like the middle of July, at the time of Dr. Baccard's brief return, something around that period of time might be appropriate, because although the sum of the witnesses there are marked as insiders, they're all comparatively short witnesses. They're not the big witnesses. So although it's always inconvenient for witnesses to come and not give evidence or to find that they're kept longer than expected, that's probably the period of time when it might be least likely to cause a major disruption. And if it's in the middle of July, it will give all parties some time to plan their use of the month of August.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If there's nothing more you want to raise, I'm just going to ask the senior legal officer to approach us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. We will rise in a moment to deal -- to consider these matters before we give a ruling as to the timetable, but we ought to hear from Mr. Tapuskovic if there's anything he would like to raise. Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, today we have broached a number of questions. I shall try and be as brief as possible. It is quite certain that the three of us - Mr. Kay, myself, and Mr. Wladimiroff - will be able very soon to present our positions and stands with respect to all the issues discussed here today. It is very difficult to speak here today without the presence of Mr. Slobodan Milosevic, but these are all questions of importance because they are questions of importance to him personally. And I'm quite certain that we can't -- won't be having a discussion here which would be in any way to his detriment, and of course, he will be receiving the transcript of the meeting so he will be able to look at that. The friends of the court have nothing against permanently cooperating with the Prosecution on all these issues, all issues which are important to your decision and to your ruling, and we shall do our best to help you with all these questions. Also, similarly, faced with this kind of situation, I can see that we will have to shift the deadline by which the presentations were to have been made with respect to Kosovo, and I am quite sure that the Trial Chamber will bear in mind the fact that the trial, in addition to being expeditious, expedient, must also be fair and just. The problem, as I see it and that stands before us at this point is the work that we have to do with the other two indictments, and we ought to keep that in mind all the time. And I should like to say the following in respect of a problem raised by Mr. Nice: For example, the position that three witnesses are to be interviewed, examined, which are linked to the things that took place in all these areas and have to do with all three indictments. I don't think that any of these witnesses should be examined before we have had a chance to study the materials for the other two indictments, although I did listen, of course, with great care to the arguments put forward by Mr. Nice, but I don't think that they should be accepted. I also hope that the Trial Chamber would adhere to the principle that it had adhered to so far, that all the 92 bis witnesses should have an opportunity of being crossed examined, or rather, the accused should have the opportunity of cross-examining these witnesses. As for the other matters, the other issues raised, some of them were linked to Rule 70. There, of course, we shall be submitting an application to the Trial Chamber, and I speak in my own name. I think that Rule 70 enables every witness to be examined here and he needn't answer questions that are confidential, on a confidential basis. But as far as I'm able to understand, this does not refer to this particular witness because, on the basis of that witness statement, there is nothing there that I can consider is confidential. You will probably have this crop up with some other witnesses that are due to appear. But you will be ruling on that, but I do consider that Rule 70 ensures full protection for all witnesses who appear in court here. And as to all the other issues, we shall do our best, our utmost to state our positions as quickly as possible, the issues raised here today. I should just perhaps like to raise one point at this juncture, and that is that on several occasions I was cautioned by the Prosecution that I had taken it upon myself to present a historical background to some of the facts related to Yugoslavia. However, studying the material linked to Kosovo, I have come up with an exhibit. It is 2611. The number is Exhibit 2611 and it has to do with Kosovo and Metohija and the historical view. And this was published by the Federal Secretariat for Information in 1978 in Yugoslavia. And -- but I have come to the opinion that it would not be in order for me to present my views at this juncture if the Prosecution indeed has these documents and can read through them. And this will be something that we will come to in due course in the future. And we are working on the expert report and expert findings to be provided by our expert historical witness. May I just say this now as far as translation is concerned: I think that the expert reports by our experts should be translated, because anybody reading the expert reports must have complete knowledge of the language he's reading in. This is professional expert terminology, legal terminology, military terminology, historical terminology, et cetera, and I don't think that Mr. Slobodan Milosevic has sufficient knowledge of the English language to be able to fully grasp the portent of the material in a language other than his own. So I think that they must be made translated and accessible to him, and of course, the decision and ruling stands that all documents must be supplied to him in his mother tongue. So that is what we had to tell you as the Trial Chamber, and if you have any suggestions to make for our work, we shall be happy to hear then. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Tapuskovic. Mr. Nice, one point is raised there. That is the question about -- amongst others, is the question of the insider witness and the appropriateness of calling one before the other parts of the case have been opened.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: First of all, they're all three of them, of course, principally focused on Kosovo and prepared on that basis, and that is the reason they were listed as part of the Kosovo case. Inevitably, and this isn't unique to these witnesses, witnesses called in Kosovo may have material that relates to other parts of the case. For example, Lord Ashdown was one and the Chamber permitted him to give the piece of evidence he was able to give that related to another part of the case while he was here, for convenience. Once these witnesses have come here once, it may, of course, be possible for them to come back again if in the event there's material that it's decided they should cover that they haven't covered, or if it's decided that material they have covered here that relates to other parts of the indictment would need further cross-examination in light of material coming available later. So there are various ways of resolving the problem. But we prepared the witness list and prepared their attendance on the basis that because they related to Kosovo we should try and bring them in as the Kosovo case, and it was only comparatively recently that the Chamber gave indications, particularly related to financial matters but I think also in relation to one other witness, that it might be more appropriate in general for such witnesses to give their evidence at a later stage. By that stage, very great steps -- not very great steps, very substantial arrangements had already been made for these witnesses to come in the Kosovo case. That includes their becoming adjusted to the process, their taking the various complex steps that two of them have had to take to deal with security issues themselves, and it would be, apart from all the other reasons that I've explained that would justify their being called now, it would be probably very difficult for them, inconvenient and possibly even risky for them, to put their evidence back as they'd be exposed for a longer period rather than a shorter to the knowledge that they are likely to be giving evidence, that because in part the information's already seeped or leaked out, than if they were giving evidence earlier. So we would press the Chamber. For all the reasons I've given, not least the reason of encouraging others, to say that any problems that may arise from their giving evidence wider than simply related to Kosovo can be dealt with in one of a number of ways that will avoid any unfavourable consequences for the accused.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And as to the incident -- as to the translations of expert reports, although we're not obliged to do so, we are as a matter of practice and course getting them translated. We would press you not to put any timetables on that because giving priority to those documents, if we use CLSS, where there are documents that are to be provided as a matter of statutory or regulatory duty is difficult. They do take some time to get translated, but they are all being translated. Your Honour, if there is any question of either putting back or asking us to put back any of the insider -- three insider witnesses beyond the summer, it might be necessary for us to look at them individually, one by one, to see again, possibly even ex parte -- or to make representations ex parte, to see the degree to which, or to examine the degree to which they're really likely to go beyond Kosovo at all. But I can't really do that in this session at the moment, for obvious reasons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We're going to adjourn now for half an hour to consider these matters. We'll give our ruling when we return. Meanwhile, we would be grateful for the senior legal officer and the registrar to attend upon us. We'll sit again at twenty past eleven.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The Trial Chamber will make the following orders in regard to the timetable, but first I shall deal with the objection made by Mr. Tapuskovic in relation to the three insider witnesses who the Prosecution propose to call as part of the Kosovo case. Subject to any further submissions which may be made in relation to calling them at this stage, the Prosecution may call those witnesses. Turning then to the timetable, the hearings will continue until the 26th of July. There will then be a break of four weeks to be utilised for preparation of the remaining sections of the case. The Trial Chamber will sit again on the 26th of August until Friday, the 6th of September, to hear the remainder of the Prosecution case on Kosovo, but there will be leave for the Prosecution to apply, if necessary, for one further week. The arrangements thereafter, such as any further adjournment for preparation before the rest of the case and the start of the rest of the case will be considered in due course when representations have been heard from the accused. The Pre-Trial Conference on the Bosnia and Croatia parts of the trial will take place on Friday, the 12th of July, at 2.30. That will be subject to the necessary arrangements being made. In the light of the present and past illnesses of the accused during this trial, the Trial Chamber, of its own motion under Rule 74 bis, orders a full medical examination of the accused and instructs the Registrar to make the necessary arrangements forthwith so that a report can be made available to the Trial Chamber by the 17th of July. Unless there are any further matters to be raised.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: No, subject to only this: Was the 12th of July originally one of the days set aside for the Plenary?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It was. If there are difficulties about it, then representations can be made and we can find a different date.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes, because on the basis that those days were not sitting days, I'd planned work on this case elsewhere for those two days. It hasn't yet become clear that they're going to be used, but they're quite important exercises that I have to engage in, and I had planned them specifically because the Court wasn't sitting then. So it might be that I would ask for that appointment to be shifted. And the only other matter of detail, when we were looking at the Novi Sad translation project, that's translation into English, not into B/C/S. But I think as a slip of the tongue, Your Honour may have said otherwise, but in fact, that's the exercise that's being performed at the Novi Sad university.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We'll consider the arrangements for the 12th of July. If we can sit that afternoon, it may be a useful exercise anyway, even if we can't deal with the Pre-Trial Conference.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. May I approach the Chamber on these timetable matters through the usual channels when I've checked what my position is on that date?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Very well. We will adjourn now until the Court can sit next.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned sine die at
